texts.title: Is the Four-Day Week Here to Stay?
texts.body:
When a mid-sized accounting firm in Halifax announced last spring that its staff would work four days a week for the same salary, many of its competitors predicted disaster. Clients, they said, would leave, deadlines would be missed, and the experiment would quietly end before the summer.

A year later, the firm's managing partner says the opposite has happened. Revenue rose by six per cent, staff turnover fell from eighteen per cent to just four, and the number of sick days taken dropped by almost half. "People simply stopped wasting time," she explains. "When you know Friday is yours, you think twice before scheduling a meeting that could have been an email."

The firm is not alone. Pilot programmes in the United Kingdom, Iceland and Spain have reported similar results, and several Canadian provinces are now studying the idea. Supporters argue that shorter weeks reduce burnout, help companies attract talent and even cut carbon emissions from commuting.

Critics, however, warn against drawing conclusions too quickly. Most pilots involve office workers whose output is difficult to measure, and companies that volunteer for such trials are likely to be enthusiastic from the start. "It works brilliantly for a twenty-person consultancy," says one labour economist. "Whether it works for a hospital, a factory or a school is a completely different question."

There is also the problem of intensity. Some employees in the Halifax firm admit that their four days now feel longer and more stressful than the five they used to work. For them, the extra day off is less a reward than a recovery period.

For now, the four-day week remains an experiment rather than a revolution. But as more organisations publish their results, the question may soon shift from whether it can work to where it works best.

glossary.turnover: the rate at which employees leave a company and are replaced
glossary.burnout: physical or mental exhaustion caused by long-term stress at work
glossary.pilot programme: a small-scale trial run before a full launch
glossary.consultancy: a company that gives expert advice to other businesses
glossary.intensity: the quality of being concentrated, demanding or extreme

questions.prompt: What is the main idea of the article?
options: The four-day week has failed in most countries.
The four-day week shows promising results, but it is unclear how widely it applies.
Canadian provinces have made the four-day week compulsory.
Accounting firms are especially suited to shorter weeks.
questions.answer: The four-day week shows promising results, but it is unclear how widely it applies.
questions.explanation: The article presents positive results, then critics' doubts about other sectors, and ends calling it 'an experiment rather than a revolution'.

questions.prompt: What happened to staff turnover at the Halifax firm?
questions.answer: It fell from 18% to 4%.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'staff turnover fell from eighteen per cent to just four'.

questions.prompt: Why does the economist mention hospitals and factories?
options: Because they already use four-day weeks.
To suggest that results from office pilots may not transfer to other workplaces.
To show that these sectors have high turnover.
Because they took part in the Spanish pilot.
questions.answer: To suggest that results from office pilots may not transfer to other workplaces.
questions.explanation: He contrasts a small consultancy with sectors where output and staffing work differently.

questions.prompt: In paragraph 4, 'volunteer for such trials' implies that the companies…
options: chose to participate and may be biased in favour.
questions.answer: chose to participate and may be biased in favour.
questions.explanation: This is selection bias: self-selected participants are 'likely to be enthusiastic from the start'.

questions.prompt: Which statement would the author most likely agree with?
options: The four-day week should be adopted immediately everywhere.
Critics of the four-day week are simply wrong.
More evidence from different sectors is needed before judging the four-day week.
questions.answer: More evidence from different sectors is needed before judging the four-day week.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph says the question will shift to 'where it works best' as more results are published.

texts.discussion: Would a four-day week work in your profession? Give two reasons for and two against.

texts.title: Why Central Banks Raise Interest Rates
texts.body:
Few announcements move financial markets as quickly as a central bank's decision on interest rates. Yet for many people the logic behind these decisions remains a mystery. Why would an institution deliberately make borrowing more expensive?

The answer lies in the central bank's main task: keeping inflation low and stable. In Canada, the Bank of Canada aims for inflation of around two per cent a year. When prices rise much faster than that, the money in people's pockets loses value, savings are eroded, and businesses struggle to plan ahead.

Raising the policy interest rate works through several channels. First, loans and mortgages become more expensive, so households borrow and spend less. Second, saving becomes more attractive, since deposits earn higher returns. Third, companies postpone investment projects because the cost of financing them has increased. Together, these effects reduce demand across the economy, which eventually slows the rise in prices.

The key word is 'eventually'. Economists estimate that a change in interest rates can take between twelve and twenty-four months to have its full effect on inflation. This delay makes central banking difficult: policymakers must act on forecasts rather than on what they can see today. If they raise rates too slowly, inflation may become entrenched; if they raise them too aggressively, they risk pushing the economy into a recession.

Higher rates also have side effects. Bond prices fall when rates rise, which can hurt pension funds and banks holding large bond portfolios. Homeowners with variable-rate mortgages may see their monthly payments increase sharply, and the currency often strengthens, making exports less competitive.

This is why central bankers often describe their job as a balancing act. Their aim is a so-called 'soft landing': bringing inflation back to target without causing a severe downturn.

glossary.policy interest rate: the key rate set by a central bank that influences all other rates
glossary.postpone: to delay to a later time
glossary.entrenched: firmly established and difficult to change
glossary.soft landing: slowing the economy enough to reduce inflation without causing a recession

questions.prompt: The text mainly explains…
options: how to invest when rates are high.
the history of the Bank of Canada.
how and why rate increases are used to control inflation, and their risks.
questions.answer: how and why rate increases are used to control inflation, and their risks.
questions.explanation: It covers the purpose, the channels, the time lag and the side effects.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT mentioned as a channel through which higher rates reduce demand?
questions.answer: Governments cut taxes.
questions.explanation: Taxes are fiscal policy and are not mentioned.

questions.prompt: Why must policymakers 'act on forecasts'?
options: Because rate changes take one to two years to affect inflation fully.
questions.answer: Because rate changes take one to two years to affect inflation fully.
questions.explanation: The time lag means today's decision affects future inflation.

questions.prompt: 'Balancing act' in the final paragraph suggests…
options: managing two risks that pull in opposite directions.
a decision taken by a committee.
questions.answer: managing two risks that pull in opposite directions.
questions.explanation: Inflation vs recession.

texts.discussion: Explain to a friend with a variable-rate mortgage why their payments have risen, in under one minute.

texts.title: The Last Train to Kingston
texts.body:
Marguerite had always believed that trains were for people with patience, and she had very little of it. So when the departure board at Union Station flickered and the 21:40 to Kingston changed from 'On time' to 'Delayed', she let out a sigh loud enough to make the man beside her look up from his newspaper.

"Forty minutes," he said, as if she had asked. "It's always forty minutes. They never say an hour, because then people would leave."

He was older than her father would have been, with a grey scarf wrapped twice around his neck and a paper cup of tea he held but never drank. She nodded politely and returned to her phone, hoping the conversation would end there. It didn't.

"Business or pleasure?"

"Neither," she said, and was surprised to hear herself continue. "My mother's moving into a care home tomorrow. I'm supposed to help her choose what to keep."

The man folded his newspaper carefully, the way people fold letters they intend to read again. "I did that for my wife," he said. "Seven years ago. Do you know what she kept? Not the jewellery, not the photographs. A wooden spoon. She said it had stirred every birthday cake our children ever had."

Marguerite laughed, and then, unexpectedly, felt her eyes sting. She thought of her mother's kitchen, of the chipped blue bowl that had held every Sunday salad of her childhood.

When the train was finally announced, the man stood up slowly and wished her luck. She realised she hadn't asked his name. By the time she turned to ask, he had disappeared into the crowd.

On the train, Marguerite didn't open her phone. She watched the dark lake slide past the window and made a list, not of things to throw away, but of things to ask her mother about.

glossary.flickered: shone unsteadily, turning on and off quickly
glossary.care home: a residential home for elderly people who need support (US: nursing home)
glossary.chipped: with a small piece broken off the edge
glossary.sting: to feel a sharp, burning sensation (here: eyes about to cry)

questions.prompt: What is the story mainly about?
options: A delayed train journey to Kingston.
A chance conversation that changes how a woman approaches a difficult family moment.
An old man's memories of his wife.
How to choose possessions when moving house.
questions.answer: A chance conversation that changes how a woman approaches a difficult family moment.
questions.explanation: The ending shows her shift from 'things to throw away' to 'things to ask her mother about'.

questions.prompt: Why did Marguerite answer 'Neither' and then keep talking?
options: She wanted to impress the man.
She was angry about the delay.
She needed to share something she was finding emotionally hard.
She thought he was a doctor.
questions.answer: She needed to share something she was finding emotionally hard.
questions.explanation: 'was surprised to hear herself continue' signals an unplanned emotional release.

questions.prompt: 'the way people fold letters they intend to read again' describes the man's…
questions.answer: gentleness and care.
questions.explanation: The simile signals tenderness and attention.

questions.prompt: What does the wooden spoon symbolise?
options: That everyday objects can carry the deepest memories.
questions.answer: That everyday objects can carry the deepest memories.
questions.explanation: It is chosen over jewellery and photographs because of the memories attached to it, and is echoed by the blue bowl.

texts.discussion: Which ordinary object from your childhood would you keep, and why? Answer using at least two past-tense forms and one relative clause.

texts.title: When Algorithms Decide Who Gets Hired
texts.body:
The promise of algorithmic hiring is seductive. Human recruiters, we are told, are tired, inconsistent and prone to bias; they favour candidates who went to their old university, who share their hobbies, or who simply have names they find easy to pronounce. An algorithm, by contrast, evaluates every application against the same criteria, never gets hungry before lunch, and can screen ten thousand CVs in the time it takes a person to read ten.

The difficulty is that algorithms learn from the past, and the past is precisely what many organisations claim they are trying to escape. A model trained on a decade of hiring decisions will, unless carefully corrected, absorb whatever patterns those decisions contained. If a company historically promoted men into engineering roles, the system may learn that attributes correlated with being male are predictors of success, even when gender itself has been removed from the data. Words such as 'captain' of a sports team, gaps in employment, or the name of a particular college can act as proxies.

Defenders of these tools rightly point out that human bias is no less real for being harder to measure. At least an algorithm can be audited; a manager's intuition cannot. This is a fair argument, but it holds only if audits actually take place, if their results are published, and if candidates have a meaningful way to challenge a decision. At present, few of these conditions are met. Most applicants rejected by an automated system never learn that software was involved, let alone why it ranked them as it did.

None of this means that algorithms should be banned from recruitment. It means that their use should be governed by the same principles we expect of any consequential decision: transparency, accountability and the right of appeal. Efficiency is a legitimate goal, but it is not a substitute for fairness, and it should never be mistaken for it.

glossary.seductive: attractive in a way that may be misleading
glossary.prone to: likely to suffer from or do something (usually negative)
glossary.proxies: (singular: proxy) things that represent or substitute for something else
glossary.audited: officially examined for accuracy or fairness

questions.prompt: What is the author's overall position?
options: Algorithms should be banned from hiring.
Algorithms are fairer than humans and should replace recruiters.
Algorithmic hiring can be useful but requires transparency, accountability and appeal.
questions.answer: Algorithmic hiring can be useful but requires transparency, accountability and appeal.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph rejects a ban but calls for governance principles.

questions.prompt: How does the author respond to the argument that algorithms can be audited?
options: Accepts it, but says it only holds if audits happen, are published and decisions can be challenged.
questions.answer: Accepts it, but says it only holds if audits happen, are published and decisions can be challenged.
questions.explanation: 'This is a fair argument, but it holds only if…' is a concession followed by conditions.

questions.prompt: Why might 'captain of a sports team' be problematic as a data point?
options: It is irrelevant to all jobs.
It may correlate with gender or background and act as an indirect proxy for bias.
It is illegal to ask about sports.
questions.answer: It may correlate with gender or background and act as an indirect proxy for bias.
questions.explanation: The text lists it among examples of proxies.

questions.prompt: 'never gets hungry before lunch' refers ironically to…
options: the idea that human judgement varies with physical state such as fatigue or hunger.
questions.answer: the idea that human judgement varies with physical state such as fatigue or hunger.
questions.explanation: It contrasts human inconsistency with machine consistency.

questions.prompt: Which rhetorical technique does the first paragraph mainly use?
options: It presents the opposing view sympathetically before critiquing it.
questions.answer: It presents the opposing view sympathetically before critiquing it.
questions.explanation: 'The promise… is seductive' sets up the counterargument the author then examines.

texts.discussion: Should candidates have a legal right to know if an algorithm rejected them? Argue your position in a short paragraph using at least one concession ('Admittedly…', 'While it is true that…').

texts.title: Northwind Capital — Q3 Portfolio Commentary
texts.body:
Summary. The Fund returned 2.4% net of fees in the third quarter, outperforming its benchmark by 60 basis points. Year-to-date performance stands at 7.9%, against 6.8% for the benchmark. Relative gains were driven primarily by our overweight position in Canadian financials and by security selection within industrials, partly offset by our underweight in energy, which rallied sharply in September.

Market environment. The quarter was characterised by elevated volatility as investors reassessed the likely path of interest rates. Following stronger-than-expected employment data in July, markets priced out two of the three rate cuts previously anticipated for the coming year. Long-term bond yields rose accordingly, weighing on interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as utilities and real estate, in which the Fund was deliberately underweight.

Portfolio activity. We initiated a position in a mid-cap logistics company whose investments in automated warehousing have, in our view, not yet been reflected in its valuation. We also reduced our exposure to two consumer-discretionary holdings, where we believe that weakening household spending poses a growing risk to earnings. Our cash allocation was increased modestly to 4% to provide flexibility should valuations become more attractive.

Outlook. While inflation has moderated, it remains above central-bank targets, and we expect monetary policy to stay restrictive for longer than consensus forecasts suggest. Against this backdrop, we continue to favour companies with strong balance sheets, pricing power and consistent free cash flow. We remain cautious on highly leveraged businesses, whose refinancing costs are likely to rise materially over the next eighteen months.

Past performance is not indicative of future results.

glossary.basis point: one hundredth of one per cent (0.01%); 60 basis points = 0.6%
glossary.overweight: holding more of a sector than the benchmark does
glossary.priced out: removed an expectation from market prices
glossary.pricing power: a company's ability to raise prices without losing customers
glossary.free cash flow: cash a company generates after paying for operations and investment
glossary.restrictive: (of monetary policy) designed to slow the economy, with high interest rates

questions.prompt: By how much did the Fund beat its benchmark in Q3?
questions.explanation: 60 basis points = 0.6 percentage points.

questions.prompt: Why did the underweight in energy hurt relative performance?
options: Energy stocks rose strongly and the Fund held less of them than the benchmark.
The Fund sold all its energy stocks at a loss.
questions.answer: Energy stocks rose strongly and the Fund held less of them than the benchmark.
questions.explanation: Being underweight a sector that rallies reduces relative return.

questions.prompt: Why did rising bond yields not hurt the Fund much?
options: The Fund held no bonds at all.
The Fund was underweight interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as utilities and real estate.
questions.answer: The Fund was underweight interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as utilities and real estate.
questions.explanation: 'in which the Fund was deliberately underweight'.

questions.prompt: What is the managers' view on interest rates compared with the market consensus?
options: Rates will fall sooner than expected.
Rates will stay high for longer than most forecasts suggest.
Rates will rise sharply next month.
questions.answer: Rates will stay high for longer than most forecasts suggest.
questions.explanation: 'restrictive for longer than consensus forecasts suggest'.

questions.prompt: 'weighing on' in paragraph 2 means…
questions.answer: putting downward pressure on.
questions.explanation: A common market-commentary verb: 'X weighed on stocks'.

texts.discussion: Summarise this commentary for a client with no financial background in three sentences.

texts.title: Sleep and the Consolidation of Memory
texts.body:
For much of the twentieth century, sleep was regarded by many scientists as a passive state: a period in which the brain, like an idle engine, simply rested. Research over the past three decades has overturned this view. It is now widely accepted that sleep plays an active role in memory consolidation, the process by which newly acquired information is stabilised and integrated into long-term storage.

The evidence comes from several directions. In behavioural studies, participants who learn a list of word pairs and then sleep typically recall more of them the following day than participants who spend the same interval awake. Crucially, the advantage persists even when the timing of testing is controlled, suggesting that the effect cannot be attributed merely to fatigue in the waking group.

Neurophysiological recordings offer a possible mechanism. During deep, slow-wave sleep, the hippocampus, a region essential for forming new memories, appears to 'replay' patterns of activity recorded during learning. These replays coincide with brief bursts of activity known as sleep spindles, which are thought to facilitate communication between the hippocampus and the neocortex. Over successive nights, memories may gradually become less dependent on the hippocampus and more firmly embedded in cortical networks.

The picture is not, however, without complications. Different types of memory may benefit from different stages of sleep: factual knowledge appears to rely heavily on slow-wave sleep, whereas some studies associate procedural skills, such as playing a musical instrument, with lighter stages. Moreover, much of the most detailed mechanistic evidence comes from studies of rodents, and its applicability to humans remains to be fully established.

For learners, the practical implications are nonetheless clear. Studying immediately before sleep, and avoiding sleep deprivation in the days after learning, are likely to improve retention, a finding with obvious relevance to anyone preparing for an examination.

glossary.consolidation: the process of making something stronger or more permanent
glossary.hippocampus: a brain region crucial for forming new memories
glossary.procedural: relating to skills and how to perform actions
glossary.rodents: animals such as mice and rats

questions.prompt: What is the central claim of the text?
options: Sleep actively helps stabilise and integrate memories, though details are still debated.
Students should sleep less before exams.
questions.answer: Sleep actively helps stabilise and integrate memories, though details are still debated.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states the thesis; paragraph 4 adds qualifications.

questions.prompt: Why is controlling 'the timing of testing' important in the behavioural studies?
options: To rule out the alternative explanation that the waking group was simply more tired.
questions.answer: To rule out the alternative explanation that the waking group was simply more tired.
questions.explanation: This eliminates a confounding variable.

questions.prompt: According to the text, what are sleep spindles thought to do?
options: Help communication between the hippocampus and the neocortex.
questions.answer: Help communication between the hippocampus and the neocortex.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3.

questions.prompt: Which limitation does the author acknowledge?
options: Sleep has no effect on procedural skills.
Much detailed evidence comes from animals and may not fully apply to humans.
The hippocampus is not involved in memory.
questions.answer: Much detailed evidence comes from animals and may not fully apply to humans.
questions.explanation: 'its applicability to humans remains to be fully established' — hedged academic language.

texts.discussion: Using hedging language ('appears to', 'is thought to', 'may'), explain in your own words how sleep might help memory.

texts.title: In Praise of Boredom
texts.body:
There was a time, not so long ago, when boredom was an ordinary feature of life rather than a problem to be solved. One waited for buses without entertainment, sat through rainy afternoons with nothing in particular to do, and endured the long, uneventful stretches that punctuated every childhood. That such experiences have all but vanished is usually counted among the conveniences of modern technology. I am no longer convinced it should be.

Boredom, after all, is not merely the absence of stimulation; it is a signal. It tells us that our present activity has ceased to engage us, and in doing so it presses us, however uncomfortably, to look for something better. The child who complains of having nothing to do is, more often than adults care to admit, on the threshold of inventing something. Deprived of that discomfort, we are also deprived of its consequences.

What has replaced it is not engagement but its imitation. The smartphone does not so much relieve boredom as anaesthetise it, offering an endless supply of novelty that demands little and rewards less. We emerge from twenty minutes of scrolling neither entertained nor rested, but with a vague sense of having been somewhere without having gone anywhere at all. The itch is scratched; the underlying restlessness remains untouched.

It would be easy, and somewhat sanctimonious, to conclude with a call to throw our devices into the sea. That is not my argument. Rather, I would suggest that boredom deserves to be tolerated, occasionally even sought out, as one might seek out silence in a noisy city. Its value lies precisely in its unproductiveness: in the room it leaves for thoughts we did not plan to have.

The mind, like a field, needs periods in which nothing appears to be growing. Whether we are still willing to leave it fallow is, perhaps, one of the quieter questions of our age.

glossary.on the threshold of: about to begin or experience something
glossary.anaesthetise: to numb, to remove the ability to feel
glossary.sanctimonious: making a show of being morally superior
glossary.fallow: (of land) left unplanted to recover its fertility

questions.prompt: What is the essayist's main argument?
options: Boredom has value as a prompt for creativity and reflection, and its disappearance is a loss.
Children today are more creative than in the past.
questions.answer: Boredom has value as a prompt for creativity and reflection, and its disappearance is a loss.
questions.explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 4 develop this; paragraph 4 explicitly rejects a device ban.

questions.prompt: 'does not so much relieve boredom as anaesthetise it' means the phone…
options: numbs the feeling of boredom without addressing its cause.
questions.answer: numbs the feeling of boredom without addressing its cause.
questions.explanation: 'Not so much X as Y' = it is more accurately Y than X.

questions.prompt: Why does the author describe a call to 'throw our devices into the sea' as 'sanctimonious'?
options: To show it is the author's real recommendation.
To anticipate and distance the essay from an extreme, morally superior position.
To mock readers who own phones.
questions.answer: To anticipate and distance the essay from an extreme, morally superior position.
questions.explanation: A pre-emptive concession that makes the more moderate claim more credible.

questions.prompt: The image of a field left 'fallow' suggests that…
options: boredom is a waste of time.
apparently unproductive periods allow later growth.
the mind should be constantly stimulated.
questions.answer: apparently unproductive periods allow later growth.
questions.explanation: Fallow land recovers fertility; the metaphor mirrors 'its value lies precisely in its unproductiveness'.

texts.discussion: Write a C2-style counter-argument: defend the view that constant access to information makes us more, not less, creative. Use at least one inversion and one 'not so much… as' structure.

texts.title: Translation, Fidelity and Power
texts.body:
The notion that a translation ought to be 'faithful' to its source is so deeply ingrained in popular discussion that it is rarely interrogated. Yet fidelity, on closer inspection, proves a remarkably elusive standard. Faithful to what, precisely: to the literal meaning of each word, to the syntactic shape of the original, to its tone, its rhythm, or the effect it produced on its first readers? These aims frequently pull in opposite directions, and every translation necessarily privileges some at the expense of others.

Translation scholars have long distinguished between strategies that 'domesticate' a text, rendering it fluent and familiar to the target audience, and those that 'foreignise' it, deliberately preserving features that mark it as originating elsewhere. Neither approach is neutral. Domestication, it has been argued, risks effacing cultural difference, presenting the foreign as merely a variant of the familiar; foreignisation, conversely, may produce a text that strikes readers as awkward, obscure or even condescending in its exoticism.

What makes these choices consequential is that they are seldom made on equal terms. Historically, the overwhelming flow of translation has been from dominant languages into less widely spoken ones, rather than the reverse. In such conditions, decisions about how to render a text are bound up with questions of prestige, access and representation: whose literature is deemed worth translating, by whom, and for which readers.

None of this is to suggest that translation is an inherently compromised activity. On the contrary, it is precisely because translators must make choices that their work is creative rather than mechanical. The point is rather that the language of fidelity tends to obscure those choices, presenting as a technical question what is, at least in part, an ethical and political one. A more honest vocabulary would acknowledge that every translation is an interpretation, and that interpretations are made by particular people, in particular places, for particular ends.

glossary.elusive: difficult to define, find or achieve

questions.prompt: What is the author's central claim?
options: 'Fidelity' hides the fact that translation involves interpretive, ethical and political choices.
Translation is a purely technical activity.
questions.answer: 'Fidelity' hides the fact that translation involves interpretive, ethical and political choices.
questions.explanation: Stated in the final paragraph: 'the language of fidelity tends to obscure those choices'.

questions.prompt: What is the function of the questions in paragraph 1?
options: To show that 'fidelity' has multiple, potentially conflicting meanings.
questions.answer: To show that 'fidelity' has multiple, potentially conflicting meanings.
questions.explanation: Rhetorical questions break the concept into competing aims.

questions.prompt: Why does the direction of translation flow matter, according to paragraph 3?
options: Because it links translation choices to unequal power, prestige and representation between languages.
Because dominant languages are easier to translate.
It doesn't; the author dismisses it.
questions.answer: Because it links translation choices to unequal power, prestige and representation between languages.
questions.explanation: 'bound up with questions of prestige, access and representation'.

questions.prompt: How does the author prevent the argument being read as an attack on translators?
options: By stating that the need for choices is what makes translation creative rather than compromised.
questions.answer: By stating that the need for choices is what makes translation creative rather than compromised.
questions.explanation: 'None of this is to suggest…' — a C2 disclaiming structure.

texts.discussion: Think of a French expression that is hard to translate into English. Should a translator domesticate or foreignise it? Justify your answer with academic hedging.

texts.title: Why £9.99 Still Works: The Psychology of Pricing
texts.body:
Walk into almost any shop and you will find prices ending in .99. Economists have long found this puzzling. A rational consumer, after all, should recognise that £9.99 is effectively £10. Yet decades of research, and the persistence of the practice itself, suggest that so-called charm pricing has a real effect on behaviour.

The most widely accepted explanation is the 'left-digit effect'. Because we read from left to right, we tend to anchor on the first digit we see. £9.99 is therefore encoded as 'nine-something' rather than 'ten', and feels meaningfully cheaper. Studies of used-car sales have found a striking illustration: cars with odometer readings just below a round number, such as 79,900 kilometres, sell for noticeably more than those just above it, even though the difference in actual wear is negligible.

Charm pricing is only one of many techniques. Retailers also rely on 'anchoring', displaying an expensive option first so that subsequent prices seem reasonable by comparison. A restaurant may list a lavish tasting menu not because it expects many customers to order it, but because it makes the main courses look modest. Similarly, the 'decoy effect' involves adding a deliberately unattractive option to steer customers towards a more profitable one. When a cinema offers a small popcorn for $5, a large for $9 and a medium for $8.50, the medium exists chiefly to make the large seem like excellent value.

Not every brand embraces these tactics. Luxury retailers often prefer round numbers, precisely because .99 signals a bargain, which is the opposite of the image they wish to project. A handbag priced at $2,000 suggests quality and confidence; one priced at $1,999.99 suggests a discount store.

As consumers become more aware of such techniques, one might expect them to lose their power. The evidence so far suggests otherwise. Knowing that a bias exists, it seems, is not the same as being immune to it.

glossary.charm pricing: setting prices just below a round number, e.g. 9.99
glossary.anchor: to rely heavily on the first piece of information received
glossary.negligible: so small that it is not important
glossary.decoy: something used to lure or mislead

questions.prompt: What is the main topic of the article?
options: How psychological pricing techniques influence consumers.
The history of the pound sterling.
questions.answer: How psychological pricing techniques influence consumers.
questions.explanation: The article surveys charm pricing, anchoring and decoys.

questions.prompt: What does the used-car example illustrate?
questions.answer: The left-digit effect.
questions.explanation: Readings just below a round number sell for more.

questions.prompt: Why might a restaurant list an expensive tasting menu?
options: To make other dishes seem reasonably priced.
questions.answer: To make other dishes seem reasonably priced.
questions.explanation: Anchoring.

questions.prompt: In the popcorn example, the medium size is a…
questions.answer: decoy.
questions.explanation: It steers customers to the large.

questions.prompt: What does the final paragraph suggest?
options: Awareness of a bias does not necessarily protect us from it.
questions.answer: Awareness of a bias does not necessarily protect us from it.
questions.explanation: Last sentence.

texts.discussion: Describe a time when you think a pricing technique influenced what you bought. Use at least two words from the glossary.

texts.title: What Remote Learning Taught Us
texts.body:
When schools and universities moved online almost overnight, many teachers expected it to be a temporary emergency measure. Several years later, it is clear that the experience changed education in lasting ways, though not always in the ways people predicted.

The most obvious lesson was that technology alone does not guarantee learning. Students with a quiet room, a reliable internet connection and their own laptop generally coped well. Those who shared a single phone with siblings, or who had to work to support their families, often fell behind. The gap between students from different backgrounds, which schools had worked hard to reduce, widened noticeably.

Teachers also discovered that long video lectures were rarely effective. Attention tends to drop sharply after about ten to fifteen minutes on screen. The most successful online courses broke content into short segments, mixed in quizzes and discussions, and gave students regular, personal feedback.

Yet there were surprising benefits too. Recorded lessons allowed students to review difficult material at their own pace, and many shy students found it easier to participate in written chat than to speak up in a crowded classroom. Today, many universities offer 'hybrid' courses that combine face-to-face teaching with online materials, and most students say they prefer this flexibility.

Perhaps the most important lesson, however, was a human one. When asked what they missed most, students rarely mentioned lectures. They talked about friends, conversations in corridors and the simple feeling of belonging to a community. Education, it turns out, is about more than the transfer of information.

texts.title: On Clarity
texts.body:
There is a persistent suspicion, in certain academic circles, that clarity is a symptom of shallowness. If an argument can be grasped on first reading, the reasoning goes, it cannot have been very profound. Difficulty becomes a badge of seriousness, and readers who struggle are quietly reminded that the fault lies with them.

I have some sympathy for the view that complex ideas resist simple expression. There are genuine thoughts that cannot be compressed into a slogan without being falsified, and a writer who strips away every qualification in pursuit of readability may end up saying something that is clear only because it is wrong. Precision has its price, and that price is sometimes paid in ease.

But the defence of difficulty is too often a defence of something else: of vagueness dressed up as depth, or of a reluctance to be pinned down. A sentence that can mean three different things is not thereby three times as profound; it is merely unfinished. The labour of clarification is not a concession to lazy readers but an obligation to oneself, for it is frequently in the attempt to say exactly what one means that one discovers whether one means anything at all.

The great stylists understood this. Their prose is often deceptively plain, yet it rewards rereading precisely because nothing in it is accidental. Clarity, in their hands, is not the absence of complexity but its mastery: the difficult thing made graspable without being made false. That is a far rarer achievement than obscurity, and a far more generous one.

glossary.badge: a sign or symbol of something
glossary.pinned down: forced to commit to a precise position
glossary.deceptively: in a way that gives a false impression
glossary.obscurity: the quality of being difficult to understand
